Newborn Care

Breastfeeding with psoriasis: care for your skin and your baby

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Psoriasis does not pass to your baby through breast milk or ordinary skin contact. Many people with psoriasis can breastfeed, including during a flare. If the nipple or breast skin is painful, or you need treatment, your dermatologist and infant-feeding team can help you find a plan that protects your health as well as your baby’s feeding.

A flare does not automatically mean stopping

Psoriasis is an inflammatory condition that can cause scaly patches, soreness, itching and sometimes cracking. It may affect the breast or nipple, but a new rash in that area should not automatically be labelled psoriasis; dermatitis, infection and other conditions can look similar.

Symptoms may change during pregnancy and after birth. If you already use treatment, arrange a postpartum review rather than stopping it without advice. Leaving significant disease untreated can also affect sleep, comfort and your ability to care for yourself.

Feeding choices should account for your symptoms and preferences. You do not have to endure severe pain to prove that you have tried hard enough, and a temporary or longer-term alternative feeding plan can be discussed when needed.

Patches may occur on the eyebrows, knees, elbows or neck as well as the breasts. Skin can burn, crack or bleed, and nails may become thickened or ridged. Weeping skin needs assessment because irritation or infection can accompany a flare.

Topical treatment depends on the product and the site

Moisturisers can reduce dryness and friction, while prescribed topical medicines may control inflammation. The choice depends on the affected area, severity and whether your baby might touch or swallow the product. A cream on the elbow is a different exposure from one on the nipple.

When a topical corticosteroid is needed on the nipple or areola, clinicians generally prefer a mild or moderate preparation for the necessary duration. Apply it as directed after a feed and gently remove residue with warm water before the next feed. Wash your hands after application and keep the baby from contacting treated areas elsewhere.

Do not use a strong steroid, coal-tar product, vitamin D analogue or another psoriasis treatment directly on the breast without checking the instructions for that exact medicine. Nor should every breast be scrubbed before every feed; unnecessary washing can further irritate skin.

Some options for more extensive psoriasis remain available

UVB phototherapy, including narrowband UVB, can be used during breastfeeding. It is a prescribed treatment with a controlled dose, not an invitation to use sunbeds or expose the baby to a treatment lamp. PUVA uses a different combination involving a light-sensitising medicine and needs separate advice.

Systemic treatments cannot be grouped together as either all safe or all forbidden. Some are unsuitable, while certain biologics have reassuring breastfeeding data. For example, current lactation references consider adalimumab and certolizumab low-risk options in appropriate circumstances.

Milk levels, oral absorption by the baby, the evidence available for that drug, infant maturity and your own disease all matter. Many biologics are injections rather than oral medicines. Do not stop an effective treatment or wean solely because the word biologic appears on the label.

Tell your baby’s clinician about treatment used during pregnancy as well as breastfeeding. Infant vaccine advice can depend on the particular medicine and exposure before birth; breastfeeding exposure should not be assumed to carry the same implications.

Breastfeeding medicine studies are often observational, so absence of a large trial does not establish either safety or harm. Ask how much is known about your exact treatment rather than assuming all systemic medicines have the same evidence.

Reduce friction and keep feeding comfortable

Choose comfortable clothing that does not rub sore patches, and change damp breast pads. A fragrance-free moisturiser agreed with your clinician may help dry skin. Avoid picking scales or applying hot compresses to an inflamed nipple.

Breast milk applied to the skin is not an established treatment for psoriasis. It should not replace an effective skin-care plan, particularly when there is cracking, weeping or possible infection.

Ask someone to observe a feed if attachment is painful. A position that avoids friction on a sore area may help. If direct feeding is too painful, discuss expressing or another feeding method while the skin is treated. Pumping can also irritate skin, so check flange fit and use comfortable suction.

A plan for milk removal should match your feeding goals and avoid both uncomfortable abrupt changes and excessive pumping. If only one side is affected, your team can help you decide how to use each breast while maintaining adequate intake.

Know when the skin needs reassessment

Seek prompt advice for increasing warmth, spreading redness, pus, fever or a painful swollen breast. Severe pain or feeling generally unwell needs timely assessment. A persistent one-sided nipple rash, ulcer, new inversion or unusual discharge should also be examined rather than repeatedly treated as a familiar flare.

At review, bring the names and strengths of all creams, tablets, injections and supplements. Ask which products can contact the nipple, how to remove them, what infant monitoring is needed and when to return if symptoms do not improve.

Your treatment plan can be adjusted as symptoms and feeding change. The goal is effective, tolerable care rather than choosing between all treatment and all breastfeeding.

Your dermatologist or maternity team may know local or online peer groups for parents living with psoriasis. Sharing practical experience can help with worry and isolation, while medicine decisions still need an individual clinical review.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Psoriasis is not contagious; breastfeeding decisions depend on symptoms and the specific medicine.

Check treatment strength, application site and infant contact rather than stopping all skin treatment.

How BeMama can help

Prepare a list of treatment names and where you apply them, and ask for both feeding support and a postpartum skin plan.

When to seek help

Fever, spreading redness, pus or worsening breast pain needs prompt assessment. A persistent one-sided nipple change should be examined.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS Specialist Pharmacy Service — Using inhaled or topical corticosteroids during breastfeeding
  • LactMed / US National Library of Medicine — Adalimumab

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Psoriasis itself is not transmitted through milk or skin contact.
  • Check each treatment rather than avoiding all medicines.
  • Prevent direct infant contact with medicated skin.
  • Pain, infection signs or a persistent unfamiliar rash need assessment.

Frequently asked questions

Will my baby catch psoriasis from breastfeeding?

No. Psoriasis is not contagious. A separate infection on the skin is a different issue and needs its own advice.

Do biologic injections always mean I must wean?

No. Certain biologics are considered compatible with breastfeeding. Your dermatologist should check the specific drug and your baby’s circumstances.

Can I put my usual psoriasis cream on the nipple?

Check first. Product strength, ingredients and the risk of direct swallowing matter, even when a treatment is suitable elsewhere on your body.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
